topic.subject: science
topic.title: Gravitation
topic.scope: universal law of gravitation, free fall, g, mass vs weight, thrust and pressure, buoyancy, Archimedes' principle

misconceptions.statement: Mass and weight are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, people use the terms interchangeably when buying groceries or checking body weight.
misconceptions.fix: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and remains constant, while weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass and changes based on location.

probe.question: If an astronaut goes to the Moon, does their mass change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they weigh less on the Moon, their mass must have decreased.

misconceptions.statement: Only large objects like the Earth exert a gravitational force.
misconceptions.why: Students only observe the effects of gravity when objects fall toward the Earth, never between everyday small objects.
misconceptions.fix: Every object in the universe with mass exerts a gravitational pull on every other object, though it is only noticeable when at least one object is very massive.

probe.question: Do two pencils lying on a table exert a gravitational force on each other?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are too small and not planets.

misconceptions.statement: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects.
misconceptions.why: Observation of falling objects like a feather and a stone in air leads to the belief that weight determines speed of fall.
misconceptions.fix: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of their mass.

probe.question: If you drop a heavy iron ball and a light plastic ball from the same height in a vacuum, which hits the ground first?
probe.wrong_answer: The iron ball, because it is heavier and gravity pulls it harder.

misconceptions.statement: Objects float in water only if they are light.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the density of an object with its total weight or mass.
misconceptions.fix: An object floats if its density is less than the density of the fluid it is placed in, regardless of its total mass.

probe.question: Why does a massive steel ship float while a small steel nail sinks?
probe.wrong_answer: The ship is light enough to float, but the nail is too heavy for its size.
